catalog_quote: §3.3: Accentual languages including English are full of “phonological enclitics” that reflect prosodic reduction of syntactic words, which are then hosted in suffix-like forms by accentually stable words (isn’t, gonna, etc.). As in many languages without accents or clear prosodic indications of word boundaries, the distinction between cliticization, affixation, and simple juxtaposition is often indeterminate or at least unprovable. ... §2.1.2: There are three phonetic tone levels, but M[id] and L[ow] are essentially positional variants of a single nonhigh tone value, resulting in a phonemic two-level tone system H[igh] versus L. ... §2.1.3: Segmental and metrical phonology is relatively simple. The sequence Cvrv (where v is any short vowel) can undergo partial syncope of the first vowel. ... §3.1.1 Syllables and metrical structure: Words are normally composed of Cv and Cvv syllables.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every quoted passage is verbatim at the stated section/page in the Zenodo PDF we hold of Heath & Tioté 2019. Deciding source: a 395-page 2019 reference grammar by an experienced Africanist fieldworker plus a native-region linguist, open access, Glottolog's sole grammar for mbre1244; its §2.1.2 'Tones and prosody' and ch.3 phonology describe a two-level tone system (M a positional variant of L), Cv/Cvv syllables and Cvrv syncope, and never posit word stress; the §3.3 sentence groups Pere with 'languages without accents or clear prosodic indications of word boundaries'. The statement is oblique rather than a flat 'Pere has no stress', but nothing in the grammar (a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/metrical) contradicts the no-word-stress reading, and the only prominence-like remarks (schwa weakening in Cvrv, pitch drop on compound medials in 'weak metrical position') are

sources.quote: 'Three tone levels are marked in the transcription, but M-tone (e.g., ā) is a predictable development from L-tone (e.g., à).' No mention of word stress or accent; the two occurrences of 'stress(es)' (txt l.587, 591) refer to syntactic tension in SVO order, not phonological stress.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2017. Pɛrɛ: a Niger-Congo language of Côte d'Ivoire of unknown affiliation. Draft manuscript, 07 July 2017. 25 pp. (Glottolog ref 547513, hh file; circulated on Academia.edu, id 33800165.)
sources.note: No tone description or inventory; about two dozen wordlist forms (taken from Creissels' and Rongier's manuscripts) carry acute, grave, macron or caron tone marks, most forms are unmarked.

tone.quote: The wordlist is a composite derived from Creisssels’ manuscript and a later unpublished manuscript of Jacques Rongier (Rongier ined.), resorted by semantic category. ... Numerals one pĩ́ dɔ́ #-do is a common element in Mande for ‘one’ but this leaves the pĩ element unexplained. two yɔ̀ g̃ ɔ́ ... three tã̄ ã̄ gɔ́ ... four na #na- is Niger-Congo (W. 263) five nū #-nu is Niger-Congo six ni sĩ́ ĩ́ ? seven ni yɔ̀ g̃ ɔ́ ? perhaps a compound of 5 + 2 ... twenty mwà fifty bí lōōlū < Dyula bi looru hundred kɛ́mɛ̀ < Dyula kɛ̀mɛ
